title: Parvati's vow and the sankalpa
word: Maha Shivaratri as a night curriculum
hookLine: Parvati makes a vow to win Shiva and keeps it, and the night of Shiva begins with a resolve said in daylight
carry: a sankalpa: the vow said in daylight, kept in the dark

cards: Long before she is Shiva's wife, Parvati is a young woman who has decided she will marry him. Shiva is deep in meditation and doesn't look up. So she makes a vow.
She goes into the mountains and takes up austerity: she lives on fruit, then only leaves, then not even leaves. That's why one of her names is Aparna, the one without even a leaf.
Then a young ascetic turns up and mocks her: why waste yourself on a wild god who lives in cremation grounds?

teach.b: Parvati won't hear it. She turns to leave. And the young ascetic becomes Shiva.
He was testing whether her vow would hold, and it did. That's why many Hindus, especially women, remember Parvati when they keep a fast to Shiva.
Such a vow, a vrata, kept for a set time, traditionally starts the same way: with a sankalpa, a resolve made on purpose and said aloud.

On the morning of Shivaratri, after a bath, someone keeping the night takes a little water into the right palm and says where they are, what day it is, who they are, and what they will do: I will keep this fast, I will keep this night.
Then they let the water go.
Why decide in the morning? Because the hours you'll need it are the hours you can't decide well.
At two in the morning almost any reason to quit sounds wise. And water, once poured, can't be poured back.

teach.h: A PERSON IS MADE OF RESOLVE.
teach.b: Behind it sits an old idea from the Chandogya Upanishad: a person is made of resolve, and what you resolve shapes what you become. A vow is also personal. Some fast completely.
Some take fruit and milk. The vow that counts is the one you actually said, and kept, the way Parvati kept hers even while someone laughed.

how: Hindus keeping Maha Shivaratri may begin the day with a bath and a sankalpa, stating their intention to keep the fast and the vigil; a priest may lead the sankalpa before a temple puja.

games.q: what does “maha shivaratri as a night curriculum” mean?
o: a goddess who gave up her vow when it got hard
Shiva's night, where you decide at midnight whether to stay
a goddess whose vow held, even when a stranger mocked it

p: a vow kept for a set time
let go, and can't be poured back

s: the ascetic who mocked Parvati was Shiva, testing her
her vow held, and he showed himself.
a sankalpa is a wish you hope comes true
it's a resolve: you say what you'll do, and then you do it.
everyone who keeps Shivaratri takes the same vow
some fast completely, some take fruit and milk. the vow that counts is the one you said.

games.q: it's the morning of Maha Shivaratri. you're not sure you can last the whole night without food. what do you do?
o: skip the vow, since you might fail.
take a vow you can really keep, and say it clearly.
promise everything and hope for the best.
games.why: vows differ from person to person. the night curriculum starts with honesty: the vow that counts is the one you actually said, and then kept.

practice: Choose one small, honest thing you'll do before tomorrow, a meal eaten slowly or ten minutes without the phone, and say it quietly the way a sankalpa is said, with where you are and what day it is, a little water in your right palm if there's a glass nearby.

Then let the water go, into a plant or a sink, and sit with what you've promised. If you pray, offer the resolve to Shiva and Parvati, or to the God you know; if you don't, the words and the water are enough.

wordCard.voice: Maha Shivaratri. Today: the sankalpa, the resolve made in the morning with water in the palm, and Parvati, who kept her vow.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sankalpa, a resolve or intention made on purpose.

carryVoice: Your line: a sankalpa is the vow said in daylight, kept in the dark. Until tomorrow.
